To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of the percutaneous drainage (PCD) procedure is a useful method of treating postoperative abscess, with a high success rate.
percutaneous drainage is an effective treatment for postoperative abscesses after abdominal surgery.

1) the prevalence of post-operative infection is higher in patients with a history of chronic disease and/or a history of smoking; 2) post-operative infection is more likely in patients with a high body mass index; 3) post-operative infection can be predicted by the number of comorbidities; 4) the risk of post-operative infection increases with the number of surgical procedures; and 5) post-operative infection increases in patients with longer operative times.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that a large proportion of patients with a post-operative abscess have an infection of the abdominal cavity, that the majority of patients have an intra-abdominal abscess that is not drained percutaneously, and that the majority of the patients with an abscess are cured by antibiotic treatment alone.
we have identified a number of predictive factors that are associated with the failure of percutaneously draining an abscess after abdominal operations.

we found no evidence that percutaneous drainage (PCD) of postoperative intra-abdominal abscesses after abdominal surgery is associated with a lower rate of recurrence or need for further intervention.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of percutaneous catheter drainage (PCD) in the treatment of intra-abdominal abscess (IAA) is safe and effective in the majority of cases.
the risk of postoperative infection after abdominal surgery is higher in patients with pre-existing diabetes and obesity, and in those who have a longer duration of surgery.
we need to be aware that the use of a single-dose prophylactic antibiotic is not enough.
